nameStory: Ithuriel's spear gets its dramatic name from Milton's famous epic poem 'Paradise Lost,' where Ithuriel was an angel who carried a spear that could reveal truth by touch. The plant's tall, straight stem topped with star-shaped flowers reminded someone of that celestial weapon. It's a wonderfully poetic name for such an elegant wildflower!
description: Ithuriel's spear is a graceful wildflower that sends up a single, tall naked stem from an underground bulb-like corm. The stem is topped with a loose cluster of purple or blue flowers that open into sharp six-pointed stars. This California native occasionally escapes gardens in New England, growing 1-3 feet tall with a distinctly elegant, sparse appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple or blue tubular flowers that open into sharp six-pointed stars, arranged in a loose spray at the top of the stem. Each flower feels papery when touched and has a subtle sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single tall, completely bare stem rising from the ground with no leaves along its length. The stem feels smooth and sturdy, like a green pencil.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves emerge only from the base of the plant, often withering before the flowers fully open. They feel soft and pliable, similar to iris leaves.

idTips.label: Underground Parts
idTips.description: Grows from a small, round corm (like a tiny potato) buried in the soil. If exposed, the corm feels firm and smooth with a papery outer layer.

habitat: In New England, this is extremely rare and found only as an occasional garden escape in disturbed areas near homes or abandoned plantings. It prefers well-drained, sandy soils in sunny locations. Given its single observation count, finding one would be like discovering a botanical treasure!

seasonality.spring: Narrow leaves emerge from the ground in early spring, looking like young grass shoots. The leaves are soft to touch and may begin yellowing as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Tall flower stems shoot up in early to mid-summer, topped with clusters of star-shaped purple or blue blooms. This is peak identification time when the distinctive naked stem and stellar flowers are unmistakable.
seasonality.fall: Plants have typically died back completely by fall, leaving no visible trace above ground. The underground corm remains dormant through the cooler months.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts visible. The plant survives as a small corm buried in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger new growth.

funFact: The underground corm is edible and tastes remarkably like a potato when cooked! Native California peoples traditionally harvested these 'grassnuts' as an important food source, roasting them in earth ovens or eating them raw - making this beautiful flower essentially a wild potato with celestial blooms.
confusionNotes: The bare stem topped with star-shaped flowers is quite distinctive, but young plants might be confused with wild onions or other bulb plants. However, Ithuriel's spear lacks the onion smell when crushed and has that characteristic six-pointed star flower shape rather than rounded umbels.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was formerly classified in the genus Brodiaea, so you might see it listed as Brodiaea laxa in older field guides or garden catalogs. The reclassification to Triteleia reflects better understanding of its genetic relationships, but the beautiful common names remain the same.
compareHints: As the only Triteleia species reported in New England, it's most similar to other bulb plants in the broader asparagus family like wild onions or star-of-Bethlehem. However, it differs by having completely bare flower stems (no leaves partway up) and distinctly six-pointed star flowers rather than the dome-shaped or rounded flower clusters of its relatives.
